entries.topicDescription: Self-contained blocks of functionality that can be passed around.

tips.title: Trailing closure syntax keeps code clean
tips.content:
When the last parameter of a function is a closure, Swift lets
you write it outside the parentheses. This is called trailing
closure syntax and it dramatically improves readability.

If the closure is the only argument, you can even drop the
parentheses entirely. This is why SwiftUI code looks so clean
— views are built with trailing closures.

For functions with multiple trailing closures (Swift 5.3+),
the first uses trailing syntax and subsequent ones are labeled.

Trailing closures are purely syntactic sugar. The behavior is
identical; it just reads more naturally, especially when the
closure body is multi-line.

tips.title: Capture lists prevent retain cycles
tips.content:
Closures capture references to variables from their surrounding
scope. When a closure captures 'self' and is stored by self,
you create a retain cycle — neither can be deallocated.

Use '[weak self]' in the capture list to break the cycle. This
makes self an optional inside the closure. You'll typically
use 'guard let self' at the top to unwrap it.

Use '[unowned self]' when you're certain self will never be nil
during the closure's lifetime. It's like a force unwrap — faster
but crashes if self is deallocated.

The general rule: use [weak self] for escaping closures stored
long-term (network callbacks, timers), and you often don't need
capture lists for non-escaping closures.

tips.title: Escaping vs non-escaping closures
tips.content:
By default, closure parameters are non-escaping — they must be
called before the function returns. The compiler enforces this,
enabling optimizations like skipping reference counting.

Mark a closure '@escaping' when it will be stored or called
after the function returns. Common cases: completion handlers,
callbacks stored in properties, and async operations.

Non-escaping closures can refer to 'self' implicitly in
structs. Escaping closures require you to write 'self.'
explicitly, reminding you about potential retain cycles.

Prefer non-escaping closures when possible. They're safer,
faster, and the compiler can reason about them better. Use
@escaping only when you truly need deferred execution.
